title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
text:
Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007. The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments.
Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap, delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around.
Four years ago, when The Batman hit cinemas to a chorus of critical acclaim for its brooding blend of detective noir and superhero spectacle, there would have been little question that the studio was all in. The film took more than $770m worldwide and seemed to promise a trilogy that might one day give Christopher Nolan’s Dark Knight triptych a run for its money. But much has changed since then.
For one thing, Matt Reeves is no longer directing the remainder of the sequel’s principal photography, having stepped away from the production in October to focus on a family matter. Steven Soderbergh has been drafted in to finish filming, though Reeves says he remains committed to the project. Nevertheless, the unexpected change of director adds another layer of uncertainty to the franchise.
Meanwhile, the takeover of Warner Bros by David Ellison’s Skydance has brought a changing of the guard at DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran departing and former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham taking charge. The new regime wants to get DC’s superhero universe moving rather faster, which may not bode well for maintaining two separate versions of Batman. Gunn and Safran had envisaged a new, non-Pattinson caped crusader appearing in a project titled The Brave and the Bold, alongside Reeves’s standalone films. Whether Latcham maintains that enthusiasm remains to be seen.
You can see why the new management might want to cut the number of Batmen in half. Gotham’s defender of the night has been something of a law unto himself for decades, with successive directors allowed to reinvent him, while Warner Bros struggled to establish a coherent universe featuring Superman, Wonder Woman and the rest of the Justice League. For a studio desperate to emulate Marvel’s success at interconnected storytelling, maintaining a separate, apparently incompatible Batman might seem like an unnecessary complication.
But would anyone really want Reeves’s Batman sharing a universe with Superman? His dark knight inhabits a grimy, rain-soaked city of corrupt politicians, mobsters and serial killers, where he is unlikely to encounter a rampaging alien warlord. The introduction of Superman would risk puncturing the film’s carefully constructed atmosphere. Reeves has managed to make Batman feel like a detective again, rather than a billionaire who occasionally takes time off to investigate local crime.
None of this necessarily means Pattinson cannot play both roles. Bond is likely to occupy a substantial chunk of his working life for the foreseeable future, but it is hardly as though Reeves’s films have been arriving at a furious rate. And Harrison Ford managed to play both Han Solo and Indiana Jones, after all. The bigger question is whether the actor really wants to spend his time leading two of the most demanding franchises in cinema, particularly when he is no longer contractually obliged to complete the Batman trilogy.
It would be ironic if Warner Bros ended up sacrificing one of its few genuinely distinctive superhero franchises just as the wider DC universe was beginning to find its feet. Pattinson may yet be persuaded to return – and the studio and Skydance should be going all out to make this happen – but after years of delays, upheaval and changing priorities, nobody can assume he will. James Bond is well known for having a licence to kill. It would be a strange turn of events if his first victim turned out to be Batman.
